input.query: Analyze the current xtool-org/xtool repository and determine exactly what Apple applications it can build from a Linux host. Focus on: supported product/platform types (iOS, macOS, etc.); whether SwiftPM packages and Xcode projects/workspaces are supported; Apple SDK/toolchain acquisition; resource compilation (storyboards, asset catalogs, Metal, Core Data); code signing, provisioning, packaging, and deployment; Linux prerequisites; explicit limitations; and evidence from README/docs/source/issues. Explain whether a native macOS .app can be cross-built on Linux, not merely whether xtool itself runs on Linux. Cite repository file paths, relevant source behavior, issue/PR links where useful, and current status/version/date.

## Verdict for Lex

**No: current xtool does not provide a supported path to cross-build a native macOS `.app` from Linux.** It can cross-compile some Swift code against the macOS SDK because its generated Darwin Swift SDK happens to contain macOS target definitions, but xtool’s application planner, bundler, signing/provisioning workflow, packaging, and deployment commands are explicitly implemented for **iOS/iPadOS applications**.

For an AppKit application such as Lex—especially one stored as an `.xcodeproj`/`.xcworkspace` and using Apple resource build tools—xtool is not an Xcode-compatible Linux build system.

Status checked against `main` on **2026-07-14**, around commit [`5c4f3bc`](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/commit/5c4f3bcb0500d8c2fc4e2f918a1372bdd7c1b08d). The latest published release is **v1.17.0, released 2026-05-17**; `main` has subsequent changes.

## What xtool actually builds

| Product/platform | Linux-host status |
|---|---|
| iPhone/iPad device `.app` | **Supported**, default target `arm64-apple-ios` |
| iPhone/iPad device `.ipa` | **Supported** |
| iOS app extensions (`.appex`) | **Supported**, with qualifications |
| iOS Simulator app | Can be **built** by selecting an iOS Simulator triple; running through xtool is macOS-only |
| Native macOS `.app` | **Not supported by xtool’s app pipeline** |
| tvOS/watchOS/visionOS | **No implementation/evidence of support** |
| Mac Catalyst | **No implementation/evidence of support** |
| Xcode project/workspace as input | **Not supported** |
| SwiftPM library package converted into an app | **Supported model** |

The project describes itself narrowly as building and deploying **iOS apps with SwiftPM**, not arbitrary Apple applications ([README, lines 1–13](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/README.md#L1-L13)). Its Linux guide likewise says “iOS app development” ([Installation-Linux.md, lines 1–7](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Documentation/xtool.docc/Installation-Linux.md#L1-L7)).

The decisive source behavior is:

* The default target triple is hard-coded to `arm64-apple-ios` ([DevCommand.swift, lines 22–47](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/DevCommand.swift#L22-L47)).
* `dev build` and `dev run` identify their input/output as a “SwiftPM-based iOS app” ([DevCommand.swift, lines 108–134](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/DevCommand.swift#L108-L134), [lines 195–201](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/DevCommand.swift#L195-L201)).
* The generated helper package declares only `.iOS(...)` ([Packer.swift, lines 20–48](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/PackLib/Packer.swift#L20-L48)).
* Deployment-target discovery looks only for the SwiftPM platform named `ios`, otherwise defaulting to iOS 13 ([Planner.swift, lines 158–176](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/PackLib/Planner.swift#L158-L176)).
* Generated app metadata is unambiguously iOS: `UIDeviceFamily`, launch-screen and interface-orientation keys, `LSRequiresIPhoneOS`, and supported platform `iPhoneOS` ([Planner.swift, lines 179–193](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/PackLib/Planner.swift#L179-L193), [Packer.swift, lines 181–201](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/PackLib/Packer.swift#L181-L201)).

A custom `--triple arm64-apple-macosx` does not turn this into macOS-app support. It changes SwiftPM’s compilation triple but does not change the iOS-only package manifest, deployment-target selection, `Info.plist`, app layout assumptions, provisioning, packaging, or deployment logic.

## SwiftPM versus Xcode projects/workspaces

### Supported input: an xtool-configured SwiftPM package

xtool inspects the package using `swift package show-dependencies` and `swift package describe`, selects an automatic library product, and wraps it in a generated executable target ([Planner.swift, lines 217–290](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/PackLib/Planner.swift#L217-L290), [Packer.swift, lines 14–77](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/PackLib/Packer.swift#L14-L77)).

Consequences:

* The root application product is expected to be a **SwiftPM automatic library product**, not an ordinary Xcode application target.
* Multiple library products require choosing one in `xtool.yml`.
* Metadata, resources, icon, entitlements and extensions are described by the small `xtool.yml` schema ([PackSchema.swift, lines 5–31](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/PackLib/PackSchema.swift#L5-L31)).
* SwiftPM source targets can include C-family sources and binary targets; a Zig core could potentially participate if independently exposed to SwiftPM in a compatible way. xtool itself does not add Zig build-system or Xcode build-phase compatibility.

### Unsupported input: existing `.xcodeproj` or `.xcworkspace`

There is no project/workspace reader feeding xtool’s Linux build pipeline. `XcodePacker` does the reverse: **on macOS only**, it generates an iOS Xcode project/workspace from the xtool SwiftPM plan ([XcodePacker.swift, lines 1–17](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/PackLib/XcodePacker.swift#L1-L17), [lines 75–120](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/PackLib/XcodePacker.swift#L75-L120)). The CLI explicitly says `generate-xcode-project` “does nothing on Linux” ([DevCommand.swift, lines 96–105](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/DevCommand.swift#L96-L105)).

Even that generated project targets `.iOS`, not macOS, and has TODOs for root resources and icons ([XcodePacker.swift, lines 75–97](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/PackLib/XcodePacker.swift#L75-L97), [lines 115–117](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/PackLib/XcodePacker.swift#L115-L117)).

The maintainer has also explained that Linux `.xcodeproj` builds remain blocked by the missing conversion to the PIF consumed by `swift-build`; a possible project-to-xtool converter was described as future work. The current macOS-build question, [Discussion #204](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/discussions/204), remains unanswered.

## SDK and toolchain acquisition

Linux setup currently requires:

1. **Swift 6.3** for the Linux distribution.
2. `usbmuxd` for physical-device communication.
3. A user-downloaded **Xcode 26 `.xip`**, requiring Apple authentication and acceptance of Apple’s license.
4. An xtool AppImage for `x86_64` or ARM64 Linux.

These are documented in [Installation-Linux.md, lines 17–69](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Documentation/xtool.docc/Installation-Linux.md#L17-L69) and [lines 71–135](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Documentation/xtool.docc/Installation-Linux.md#L71-L135). Windows support means **WSL**, with USBIPD required for USB device access ([lines 11–15](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Documentation/xtool.docc/Installation-Linux.md#L11-L15)).

`xtool setup`/`xtool sdk`:

* Extracts a provided `Xcode.xip` or reads `Xcode.app`.
* Copies selected Xcode toolchain libraries and SDK/platform contents.
* Downloads xtool’s Linux Darwin toolset, currently `darwin-tools-linux-llvm` 1.0.1.
* Configures `ld64.lld` and installs the result using SwiftPM’s `swift sdk install`.

See [SDKBuilder.swift, lines 59–107](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKBuilder.swift#L59-L107), [lines 132–160](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKBuilder.swift#L132-L160), and [lines 172–220](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKBuilder.swift#L172-L220).

Notably, the produced Swift SDK defines:

```text
arm64-apple-ios
arm64-apple-ios-simulator
x86_64-apple-ios-simulator
arm64-apple-macosx
x86_64-apple-macosx
```

([SDKBuilder.swift, lines 152–160](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKBuilder.swift#L152-L160)).

That is evidence of **macOS Swift cross-compilation capability in the underlying SDK**, not evidence of a complete macOS application builder. The SDK extraction includes only iPhoneOS, iPhoneSimulator, and MacOSX platform subsets ([SDKBuilder.swift, lines 496–512](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKBuilder.swift#L496-L512)); it excludes tvOS, watchOS and visionOS.

There is also a licensing consideration: xtool does not redistribute Apple’s SDK; the user supplies Xcode. Apple’s license restrictions may matter when using those SDKs on non-Apple hardware. That is independent of technical capability.

## Resources and Apple build tools

xtool’s non-Xcode packer handles:

* SwiftPM-generated `.bundle` resource bundles.
* Dynamic binary-target frameworks/xcframework products.
* Dynamic SwiftPM libraries.
* Arbitrary files listed under `resources:` in `xtool.yml`.
* One prebuilt PNG icon copied into the app root.
* A supplied `Info.plist`.

The implementation merely copies these outputs/files into the bundle ([Packer.swift, lines 120–180](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/PackLib/Packer.swift#L120-L180)). The icon schema explicitly accepts only a `.png` path ([PackSchema.swift, lines 69–74](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/PackLib/PackSchema.swift#L69-L74)).

There is **no invocation or implementation** for Apple’s resource compilers:

| Resource | Current xtool behavior |
|---|---|
| SwiftPM `.process`/`.copy` resources | Relies on SwiftPM’s generated bundle; then copies it |
| Plain files / precompiled resources | Can copy them via `xtool.yml` |
| Storyboards / XIBs | No `ibtool` equivalent or invocation |
| Asset catalogs (`.xcassets`) | No `actool` equivalent or invocation |
| Metal sources | No `metal`/`metallib` compiler pipeline |
| Core Data models | No `momc`/`mapc` pipeline |
| Localized Xcode resources | No Xcode build-rule processing |
| Arbitrary Xcode build phases/scripts | Not interpreted |
| macOS nib/menu/AppKit resource layout | Not implemented |

Therefore an AppKit application using storyboards/XIBs, asset catalogs, compiled Core Data models, Metal shaders, or Xcode-generated resources would need those artifacts precompiled externally and manually copied—and the surrounding macOS app pipeline would still be missing.

## Signing, provisioning, packaging, and deployment

For supported iOS applications, xtool provides a substantial workflow:

* Authentication using an App Store Connect API key for paid teams or password/2FA via Apple private APIs ([Installation-Linux.md, lines 93–116](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Documentation/xtool.docc/Installation-Linux.md#L93-L116)).
* Apple Developer Services provisioning.
* App-ID/device/profile/certificate handling.
* Rewriting bundle IDs and embedding `embedded.mobileprovision`.
* Cross-platform Mach-O code signing through `zsign`/Zupersign.
* `.ipa` creation using the `Payload/<name>.app` layout.
* USB or network installation on an iOS device.
* iOS simulator installation on macOS through `xcrun simctl`.

Provisioning and profile embedding are visible in [AutoSigner.swift, lines 45–96](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XKit/Signer/AutoSigner.swift#L45-L96). `.ipa` packaging is implemented in [DevCommand.swift, lines 136–191](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/DevCommand.swift#L136-L191). Physical installation unpacks/repackages a `Payload`, signs it, and sends it through the mobile-device installer ([IntegratedInstaller.swift, lines 194–231](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XKit/Integration/IntegratedInstaller.swift#L194-L231), [lines 261–289](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XKit/Integration/IntegratedInstaller.swift#L261-L289)).

Limitations relevant to judging a macOS app:

* This is **iOS development provisioning**, not Developer ID, Mac App Store, hardened-runtime, sandbox-distribution, or notarization support.
* It packages `.ipa`, not `.pkg`, `.dmg`, or a distributable macOS archive.
* There is no macOS deployment/launch command.
* The simulator runner is compiled only on macOS and calls `xcrun simctl` ([DevCommand.swift, lines 284–303](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/DevCommand.swift#L284-L303)).
* App Store Connect upload remains outside the demonstrated workflow.
* ExtensionKit is explicitly unsupported; [issue #138](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/issues/138) tracks it ([Appex.md, lines 75–81](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Documentation/xtool.docc/Appex.md#L75-L81)).
* Multi-bundle custom entitlement signing currently contains a documented temporary hack that keeps only the root app’s entitlement mapping; [issue #131](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/issues/131) is referenced in source ([SignerImpl.swift, lines 149–163](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XKit/Signer/SignerImpl.swift#L149-L163)).

## Linux prerequisites and operational constraints

At minimum:

* Supported Linux environment or WSL.
* Swift 6.3.
* A compatible xtool AppImage architecture.
* Xcode 26 `.xip`, downloaded manually from Apple.
* Sufficient storage to extract Xcode and install the reduced Swift SDK.
* `usbmuxd` for physical iOS deployment.
* WSL USBIPD when using a USB-connected device through Windows.

Building xtool itself additionally uses Ubuntu 22.04/Jammy, C build tools, OpenSSL, XML, curl, zip/unzip, LZMA/zlib and libimobiledevice components; the repository’s reference container lists these dependencies ([Dockerfile, lines 1–21](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Dockerfile#L1-L21), [lines 24–65](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Dockerfile#L24-L65)). Docker cannot use AppImage FUSE directly and needs host `usbmuxd` forwarding for devices ([Dockerfile, lines 82–93](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Dockerfile#L82-L93), [Linux/README.md, lines 9–24](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Linux/README.md#L9-L24)).

## Practical assessment for Lex

For a local Lex repository combining Swift/AppKit, Zig and an Xcode project:

1. **AppKit is the critical blocker:** xtool does not plan or package a macOS app.
2. **An Xcode project/workspace is not accepted as build input.**
3. **Xcode build phases that invoke Zig would not run.**
4. **Apple resource compilation is absent.**
5. **macOS signing, hardened runtime, notarization and packaging are absent.**
6. The macOS SDK entries may let you manually use `swift build --swift-sdk ...` to test whether a carefully structured SwiftPM target and its Zig linkage can produce a macOS Mach-O executable. That is a lower-level experiment, **not an xtool-built native macOS `.app`**.
7. Even a source-only SwiftPM/AppKit package would require a separate macOS-specific bundler, plist/resource pipeline, signing/notarization implementation and launcher/deployer.

Accordingly, **xtool should be classified as a cross-platform SwiftPM-based iOS app tool with incidental macOS compilation SDK support—not as a Linux-to-macOS application cross-builder.**

## Feasibility classification

**Plausible experiment, not supported.**

The current SDK artifact contains nearly all of the low-level pieces needed to attempt an `arm64-apple-macosx` build on Linux: the macOS SDK, Apple Swift runtime/resource libraries, Clang importer resources, and Linux-hosted `ld64.lld`. The strongest evidence is that xtool explicitly declares macOS target triples in its generated Swift SDK.

However, xtool’s documented and tested product is still **iOS development**. There is no macOS build, bundle, signing, launch, or notarization pipeline, and no current test/example proving an AppKit executable builds from Linux. Treat success as an unvalidated toolchain experiment.

## Installing and selecting the SDK

`xtool setup` is only a convenience wrapper:

```bash
xtool setup
```

It authenticates, then installs the SDK; its own help says this is equivalent to:

```bash
xtool auth
xtool sdk
```

[`SetupCommand.swift` lines 5–17](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SetupCommand.swift#L5-L17)

The explicit SDK interfaces are:

```bash
# Build an SDK without installing it:
xtool sdk build /path/to/Xcode.xip /output/directory
# Result: /output/directory/darwin.xtoolsdk

# Install from Xcode or an already-built SDK:
xtool sdk install /path/to/Xcode.xip
xtool sdk install /path/to/Xcode.app
xtool sdk install /path/to/darwin.xtoolsdk

# "install" is the default sdk subcommand, so this also works:
xtool sdk /path/to/Xcode.xip

xtool sdk status
xtool sdk remove
```

These command names, arguments, and accepted extensions are defined in [`SDKCommand.swift` lines 10–55](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKCommand.swift#L10-L55) and [`81–125`](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKCommand.swift#L81-L125).

Installation delegates to SwiftPM rather than copying directly:

```bash
swift sdk install /path/to/darwin.artifactbundle
```

[`SDKCommand.swift` lines 144–160](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKCommand.swift#L144-L160)

Inspection/selection interfaces are therefore SwiftPM’s:

```bash
swift sdk list
# expected SDK ID:
# darwin

swift sdk configure darwin arm64-apple-macosx --show-configuration
```

xtool itself uses the equivalent iOS query to locate the installed bundle at [`SDKCommand.swift` lines 177–208](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKCommand.swift#L177-L208). The Linux guide confirms `swift sdk list` should print `darwin` at [`Installation-Linux.md` lines 118–135](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Documentation/xtool.docc/Installation-Linux.md#L118-L135).

For SwiftPM, select the macOS definition with:

```bash
swift build --swift-sdk arm64-apple-macosx
```

xtool uses precisely this target-triple-as-SDK-selector model: [`BuildSettings.swift` lines 29–35](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/PackLib/BuildSettings.swift#L29-L35). There is no xtool wrapper specifically for a standalone `swiftc` command; direct `swiftc` use requires manually extracting the paths/options from `swift sdk configure ... --show-configuration`.

## What the generated SDK contains

The builder deliberately retains:

- Xcode’s `usr/lib/swift`
- `usr/lib/swift_static`
- Clang resources
- iPhoneOS, iPhoneSimulator, **and MacOSX SDKs**
- each platform’s `Developer/Library/Frameworks`
- private frameworks
- `Developer/usr/lib`

See the allowlist in [`SDKBuilder.swift` lines 496–512](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKBuilder.swift#L496-L512).

It finds the MacOSX SDK and emits both:

```text
arm64-apple-macosx
x86_64-apple-macosx
```

[`SDKBuilder.swift` lines 99–107](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKBuilder.swift#L99-L107), [`152–160`](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKBuilder.swift#L152-L160)

Each triple points at:

- the corresponding platform SDK root;
- platform include/library paths;
- Xcode’s dynamic Swift resources;
- Xcode’s static Swift resources;
- xtool’s linker toolset.

[`SDKBuilder.swift` lines 88–96](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKBuilder.swift#L88-L96)

Consequently, ordinary contents of `MacOSX.sdk/System/Library/Frameworks` and its module maps are copied wholesale, not selected framework-by-framework. That should include:

- `AppKit`
- `ApplicationServices`
- `Carbon`
- `Foundation`
- `IOKit`, including the `IOKit.hid` submodule if the Xcode SDK’s module map defines it
- `ServiceManagement`

The repository does not enumerate or test those six imports individually, so their availability is inferred from copying the full MacOSX SDK, not directly asserted by xtool.

The installer replaces the removed Xcode Clang resource headers with the Linux host Clang’s headers, at [`SDKCommand.swift` lines 153–175](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKCommand.swift#L153-L175). That is important for a C bridging header.

## Compiler and linker viability

The SDK’s toolset is explicitly:

```json
{
  "rootPath": "toolset/bin",
  "linker": { "path": "ld64.lld" },
  "swiftCompiler": {
    "extraCLIOptions": [
      "-Xfrontend", "-enable-cross-import-overlays",
      "-use-ld=lld"
    ]
  }
}
```

[`SDKBuilder.swift` lines 132–150](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKBuilder.swift#L132-L150)

That `ld64.lld` is a Linux-hosted LLVM linker, built alongside `dsymutil` and Darwin `libtool`. The toolset build renames LLVM’s `lld` to `ld64.lld` at [`darwin-tools-linux-llvm/build.sh` lines 14–38](https://github.com/xtool-org/darwin-tools-linux-llvm/blob/main/build.sh#L14-L38).

Therefore, for a simple executable:

- **SwiftPM is the best-supported invocation layer.**
- `arm64-apple-macosx` is a first-class SDK definition.
- Framework linkage can be expressed through SwiftPM linker settings or `-Xlinker`.
- A prebuilt arm64 Mach-O `.a` should be accepted by `ld64.lld` if its members and symbols are compatible.
- It must be a real static archive containing arm64 Mach-O objects, not a Linux ELF archive. Zig’s `zig ar` output format is less important than the contained object format.
- The archive must not require unshipped libraries, unsupported relocations, or incompatible deployment versions.

A minimal SwiftPM link setup would look conceptually like:

```swift
.executableTarget(
    name: "Lex",
    cSettings: [
        // Prefer a normal C target/module map over trying to force a
        // bridging header through SwiftPM.
    ],
    linkerSettings: [
        .unsafeFlags([
            "/absolute/path/to/liblex.a",
            "-Xlinker", "-framework", "-Xlinker", "AppKit",
            "-Xlinker", "-framework", "-Xlinker", "ApplicationServices",
            "-Xlinker", "-framework", "-Xlinker", "Carbon",
            "-Xlinker", "-framework", "-Xlinker", "Foundation",
            "-Xlinker", "-framework", "-Xlinker", "IOKit",
            "-Xlinker", "-framework", "-Xlinker", "ServiceManagement",
        ])
    ]
)
```

Then:

```bash
swift build -c release --swift-sdk arm64-apple-macosx -v
```

Direct `swiftc` is also technically conceivable, but `--swift-sdk` belongs to SwiftPM’s driver interface. For raw `swiftc`, obtain the SDK root, Swift resource path, library search paths, and `ld64.lld` path from:

```bash
swift sdk configure darwin arm64-apple-macosx --show-configuration
```

Then manually pass `-target`, `-sdk`, `-resource-dir`, framework/library options, bridging-header options, and LLD selection. That path is much easier to get subtly wrong than SwiftPM.

## Likely blockers

### 1. Swift/toolchain version compatibility

The Linux documentation currently requires Swift 6.3 and Xcode 26 at [`Installation-Linux.md` lines 17–27](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Documentation/xtool.docc/Installation-Linux.md#L17-L27) and [`63–65`](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Documentation/xtool.docc/Installation-Linux.md#L63-L65). Apple `.swiftmodule` and `.swiftinterface` compatibility, overlays, and runtime ABI must match closely enough. Using an arbitrary Swift.org/Xcode combination is a likely failure source.

### 2. C bridging header integration

A raw `swiftc -import-objc-header Bridging.h` experiment may work, but SwiftPM does not model Xcode-style application bridging headers directly. A small C target with public headers/module map is usually safer. The SDK repairs Clang’s builtin headers, but that does not guarantee every Apple SDK Clang module imports cleanly under Linux.

### 3. Clang module-map and framework-overlay differences

The SDK enables cross-import overlays specifically because this has been a compatibility issue, at [`SDKBuilder.swift` lines 139–143](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKBuilder.swift#L139-L143). AppKit and Foundation are mainstream candidates; old umbrella frameworks and nested modules such as `Carbon`, `ApplicationServices`, and especially `IOKit.hid` are more likely to expose module-map assumptions tied to Apple Clang.

Potential mitigations include importing `IOKit` rather than `IOKit.hid`, or exposing the required HID declarations through the C module instead.

### 4. Linker compatibility gaps

`ld64.lld` is present, but it is not Apple `ld`. A simple executable plus static archive is within its intended scope; unusual Objective-C metadata, linker directives, archive formats, autolink entries, deployment-version load commands, or Apple-specific linker flags can still fail.

The archive must have the architecture you select:

```bash
llvm-ar t liblex.a
# Inspect each object with an available Mach-O inspection tool.
```

Duplicate Swift/Clang runtimes in the Zig archive should be avoided.

### 5. Dynamic Swift runtime deployment

The SDK includes Apple Swift runtime libraries and resource directories via [`SDKBuilder.swift` lines 91–95](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKBuilder.swift#L91-L95). For a normal modern macOS deployment, the executable generally links against OS-provided Swift dylibs rather than embedding a Linux runtime. The toolset is therefore sufficient for linking, but xtool has no macOS `swift-stdlib-tool` bundle-copy phase for deployment to older systems.

### 6. No macOS bundle pipeline

`xtool dev build` accepts a custom triple, but its implementation and help explicitly call the result an iOS app and default to `arm64-apple-ios`: [`DevCommand.swift` lines 22–48](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/DevCommand.swift#L22-L48) and [`108–134`](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/DevCommand.swift#L108-L134). Its run/install code targets iOS devices or iOS Simulator, not macOS, at [`195–266`](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/DevCommand.swift#L195-L266).

Manually creating:

```text
Lex.app/
└── Contents/
    ├── Info.plist
    └── MacOS/
        └── Lex
```

is therefore reasonable, but entirely outside xtool’s supported packer.

## Signing

xtool depends on its fork of `zsign` through `Zupersign`: [`Package.swift` lines 43–46](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Package.swift#L43-L46) and [`108–119`](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Package.swift#L108-L119).

The low-level wrapper does expose an ad-hoc identity and signs a bundle path:

```swift
case adhoc
```

[`SignerImpl.swift` lines 34–37](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XKit/Signer/SignerImpl.swift#L34-L37), with the empty-certificate implementation at [`97–111`](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XKit/Signer/SignerImpl.swift#L97-L111).

But xtool only invokes that ad-hoc mode internally when applying entitlements during its app packer, at [`DevCommand.swift` lines 68–90](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/DevCommand.swift#L68-L90). There is no public `xtool codesign` command for an arbitrary macOS bundle.

More importantly, the integrated real-signing path is unmistakably iOS-oriented:

- provisions through Developer Services;
- writes `embedded.mobileprovision`;
- uses iOS provisioning entitlements/certificates.

[`AutoSigner.swift` lines 45–93](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XKit/Signer/AutoSigner.swift#L45-L93)

The zsign fork describes itself as a cross-platform signer “for iOS 12+,” accepts mobile provisioning profiles, and documents IPA signing and ad-hoc mode at [`zsign/README.md` lines 1–2](https://github.com/xtool-org/zsign/blob/master/README.md#L1-L2), [`62–88`](https://github.com/xtool-org/zsign/blob/master/README.md#L62-L88), and [`96–129`](https://github.com/xtool-org/zsign/blob/master/README.md#L96-L129). “Supporting macOS” there means the signer runs on macOS, not evidence that it produces correct Developer ID/hardened-runtime signatures for macOS distribution.

Thus:

- **Ad-hoc Mach-O signing:** technically plausible through zsign’s generic Mach-O machinery, but unproven for a `Contents/` macOS bundle in xtool.
- **Developer ID Application signing:** not an exposed xtool workflow.
- **Hardened runtime:** no demonstrated support/configuration.
- **Notarization/stapling:** no xtool implementation.
- **Mac App Store signing:** no macOS provisioning/package pipeline.

For dependable macOS signing, transfer the unsigned bundle to macOS and use Apple’s `codesign`, then `notarytool` and `stapler` as appropriate.

## Evidence from tests and examples

There is no current repository test for Linux-to-macOS compilation. The only test file exercises SDK path matching, not compilation or linking: [`MatcherTests.swift` lines 1–52](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Tests/XToolTests/MatcherTests.swift#L1-L52).

The tutorial exclusively demonstrates iOS and explicitly describes the SDK as containing modules such as UIKit and SwiftUI, invoking:

```bash
swift build --swift-sdk arm64-apple-ios
```

[`First-app.tutorial` lines 32–37](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Documentation/xtool.docc/First-app.tutorial#L32-L37)

The README likewise scopes the product claims to iOS building and signing: [`README.md` lines 1–13](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/README.md#L1-L13). The deprecated predecessor SDK also documents only the iOS invocation despite originally being described more broadly: [`swift-sdk-darwin/README.md` lines 24–38](https://github.com/kabiroberai/swift-sdk-darwin/blob/main/README.md#L24-L38).

## Practical outcome distinction

| Outcome | Classification |
|---|---|
| Compile one Swift/AppKit source and Zig arm64 archive into a Mach-O executable | **Plausible experiment** |
| Manually place it into `Lex.app/Contents/MacOS` with `Info.plist` | **Plausible; ordinary filesystem packaging** |
| Produce an unsigned `.app` artifact for transfer to a Mac | **Plausible experiment** |
| Produce an ad-hoc-signed bundle wholly on Linux | **Plausible but unvalidated; not an xtool-supported macOS workflow** |
| Run locally after signing on the destination Mac | **Likely if compilation succeeds and macOS signing/Gatekeeper requirements are handled there** |
| Produce a normally distributable Developer ID app on Linux using xtool | **Unsupported** |
| Produce a hardened, notarized, stapled app using xtool/Linux alone | **Not available** |
| Mac App Store-ready package | **Not available** |

The narrow low-level experiment is therefore **not impossible**: the explicit `arm64-apple-macosx` SDK entry, MacOSX SDK copy, Swift runtime paths, and `ld64.lld` are deliberate enabling infrastructure. But it remains **unsupported and unproven**, with module-import compatibility and signing/distribution—not basic bundle layout—the principal risks.

Hi folks! A few months ago I shared my [Swift SDK for Darwin](https://forums.swift.org/t/introducing-an-sdk-for-building-ios-macos-apps-on-linux-experimental/66233) , which allows you to build iOS Swift Packages on Linux, amongst other things. I mentioned that a lot of work still needed to be done, such as handling codesigning, packaging, and bundling.

I'm super excited to share that we've finally reached the point where all of these things are now possible with cross-platform, open source software. Enter, xtool!

<https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool>

##  About

xtool does a lot of things (because Xcode does a lot of things :sweat_smile: ) but the headline features are

:white_check_mark: Build a SwiftPM package into an iOS app

:white_check_mark: Sign and install iOS apps

:white_check_mark: Interact with Apple Developer Services programmatically

This means it's finally possible to **build and deploy iOS apps from Linux and Windows (WSL)** . At the same time, xtool is SwiftPM-based and fully declarative, which means you can also use it to **replace Xcode on macOS** for building iOS software!

[A screenshot of xtool being invoked from VSCode A screenshot of xtool being invoked from VSCode 1920×1526 141 KB](https://global.discourse-cdn.com/swift/original/3X/c/9/c9f681035b60b7f94f3d3bc4a6120ce26142b845.jpeg "A screenshot of xtool being invoked from VSCode")

##  Using xtool

I put together some DocC Articles + a DocC Tutorial on how to get started with xtool. You can find these at [xtool.sh](https://xtool.sh) .

Gotchas

The aim so far has been to flesh out the core functionality in a typical build-run-edit loop for an iOS application. There's some things that are infeasible outside macOS, and others that are possible but still need to be implemented:

* **Interface builder:** would require a lot of effort to replicate, probably not worth it since SwiftUI mostly supersedes it at this point
* **Asset catalogs:** require reverse engineering to implement, might be worth it. You can still add images as raw files in the absence of asset catalogs, it's just less efficient.
* **Proprietary macros:** The ones that are also in the Linux toolchain (e.g. `@Observable` ) work just fine, but Apple-proprietary macros (such as the SwiftData ones) will need to be reverse-engineered and rebuilt from source if we want them to work. Or Apple could ship these as [WebAssembly Macros](https://forums.swift.org/t/poc-improving-macro-build-times-with-webassembly/70967) which would make them host-independent :folded_hands:
* **App Extensions:** Right now you can only build "Application"-type targets. I think App Extensions should be easy to implement as an addition to the `xtool.yml` spec, but just require engineering effort.
* **LLDB debugging** : this used to be pretty easy before iOS 17, and xtool has all of the pieces in place to support lldb with those old versions, but Apple has recently made a number of changes to the way you invoke LLDB's `debugserver` on iOS. There are a few modern tools that support the new approach (notably [pymobiledevice3](https://github.com/doronz88/pymobiledevice3) ), and it's already possible to use these tools to connect to lldb, but I definitely want to integrate this into xtool down the road. This will require a good amount of work since the new RemoteXPC protocol is entirely different from the legacy mechanism, but it'll probably be necessary in the future for other functionality as well.
* **App Store deployment** : You can build and run on your own device with xtool, but it doesn't let you deploy builds to App Store Connect yet. Luckily 1) iTMSTransporter is cross-platform and 2) we have all the other infra in place to interact with the ASC API, so this should be achievable too, but remains to be done.

xtool is a culmination of 8 years of work around iOS app deployment (the commit history has some nuggets!) but I'm the sole developer on this project and replicating Xcode is a massive undertaking. Now that I'm ready to share the project more widely, I'd be very happy to accept external contributions to flesh out the feature set. And if you end up using xtool, please let me know!

# xtool

Cross-platform Xcode replacement. Build and deploy iOS apps with SwiftPM on Linux, Windows, and macOS.

## Overview

xtool is a cross-platform (Linux/WSL/macOS) tool that replicates Xcode functionality with open standards.

✅ Build a SwiftPM package into an iOS app

✅ Sign and install iOS apps

✅ Interact with Apple Developer Services programmatically

## Getting Started

1. Follow the guide to install `xtool`
   
    + [Installation (Linux/Windows)](https://xtool.sh/documentation/xtooldocs/installation-linux)
    + [Installation (macOS)](https://xtool.sh/documentation/xtooldocs/installation-macos)
2. Create and run your first xtool-powered app by following the [tutorial](https://xtool.sh/tutorials/xtooldocs/first-app) !

## Examples

### Screenshot

A screenshot of xtool being invoked from VSCode

### Command line interface

```
$ xtool --help
OVERVIEW: Cross-platform Xcode replacement

USAGE: xtool < subcommand > 

OPTIONS:
  -h, --help              Show help information.

CONFIGURATION SUBCOMMANDS:
  setup                   Set up xtool for iOS development
  auth                    Manage Apple Developer Services authentication
  sdk                     Manage the Darwin Swift SDK

DEVELOPMENT SUBCOMMANDS:
  new                     Create a new xtool SwiftPM project
  dev                     Build and run an xtool SwiftPM project
  ds                      Interact with Apple Developer Services

DEVICE SUBCOMMANDS:
  devices                 List devices
  install                 Install an ipa file to your device
  uninstall               Uninstall an installed app
  launch                  Launch an installed app

  See ' xtool help <subcommand> ' for detailed help.
```

### Library

xtool includes a library that you can use to interact with Apple Developer Services, iOS devices, and more from your own app. You can use this by adding `XKit` as a SwiftPM dependency.

```
// target dependency:
 . product ( name : " XKit " , package : " xtool " )
```

# Verdict: not directly, but an unsigned cross-build is plausible

**xtool cannot currently build Lex through its supported `xtool dev build` workflow.** That workflow is specifically designed for **SwiftPM-based iOS applications**, including iOS bundle metadata, provisioning, signing, IPA packaging, and device installation—not native macOS apps.

However, xtool generates a Darwin Swift SDK containing the macOS SDK and Linux-hosted linker. That SDK could potentially serve as the low-level toolchain for manually cross-compiling Lex on Linux.

| Goal | Feasibility |
|---|---|
| Run `xtool dev build` and get `Lex.app` | **No** |
| Use xtool’s SDK to compile Lex’s AppKit executable | **Plausible, experimental** |
| Construct an unsigned `Lex.app` on Linux | **Plausible** |
| Ad-hoc sign Lex reliably on Linux | **Unsupported/unverified** |
| Run or test Lex on Linux | **Impossible** |
| Produce a Developer ID signed/notarized release | **No; requires macOS tooling** |

## Why xtool itself does not support it

xtool describes and implements its app workflow as:

- Building a SwiftPM package into an **iOS app**
- Signing and installing **iOS apps**
- Producing an `.ipa`
- Using iOS deployment targets and iPhone-specific `Info.plist` metadata

This is explicit in the [xtool README](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/README.md#L1-L13), its [development command](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/DevCommand.swift#L22-L48), and its [generated package configuration](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/PackLib/Packer.swift#L20-L48).

Supplying `--triple arm64-apple-macosx` would change the compiler target, but it would not replace xtool’s iOS bundle layout, metadata, signing, packaging, or deployment behavior.

There is also no documented or tested Linux-to-macOS application example in the repository.

## Why Lex nevertheless has a reasonable experimental path

Lex is unusually simple for a macOS application:

- One Swift source file importing AppKit, Carbon, and ServiceManagement: [Lex.swift](macos/Lex.swift#L1-L28)
- A small C bridging header: [lex.h](src/lex.h#L1-L50)
- One Zig static library
- A manually maintained bundle and `Info.plist`: [Info.plist](macos/Lex.app/Contents/Info.plist#L1-L22)
- No Xcode project, storyboard, XIB, asset catalog, Metal source, or Core Data model

The existing build already compiles directly with `swiftc` rather than `xcodebuild`: [build.zig](build.zig#L99-L118). That avoids most of xtool’s usual macOS blockers.

More importantly, xtool’s generated Darwin Swift SDK explicitly defines:

- `arm64-apple-macosx`
- `x86_64-apple-macosx`

See [SDKBuilder.swift](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKBuilder.swift#L152-L160). It also copies the MacOSX SDK and framework directories, including the SDK content needed for AppKit, Carbon, and ServiceManagement: [SDKBuilder allowlist](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKBuilder.swift#L496-L512).

The toolset configures a Linux-hosted `ld64.lld` Darwin linker: [SDKBuilder toolset configuration](https://github.com/xtool-org/xtool/blob/main/Sources/XToolSupport/SDKBuilder.swift#L132-L150).

Therefore this pipeline is technically plausible:

```diagram
╭──────────────╮
│ Zig on Linux │
╰──────┬───────╯
       │ arm64 macOS static archive
       ▼
╭─────────────────────────────────╮
│ xtool-generated Darwin Swift SDK│
│ Swift compiler + macOS SDK      │
│ + ld64.lld                      │
╰───────────────┬─────────────────╯
                │ unsigned Mach-O executable
                ▼
╭─────────────────────────────────╮
│ Lex.app/Contents/MacOS/Lex      │
│ + existing Info.plist           │
╰───────────────┬─────────────────╯
                │ transfer to macOS
                ▼
╭─────────────────────────────────╮
│ codesign and runtime testing    │
╰─────────────────────────────────╯
```

## Required changes and likely problems

The existing build deliberately stops the app pipeline on non-macOS hosts: [build.zig](build.zig#L47-L63). A Linux cross-build experiment would need a separate branch in that build logic.

Likely technical risks are:

1. **Swift version compatibility**  
   Current xtool documentation requires Swift 6.3 and an Xcode 26 `.xip`. The Linux Swift compiler must be compatible with the Swift modules and interfaces in that Xcode SDK.

2. **Bridging-header support**  
   The existing `-import-objc-header src/lex.h` might work with raw `swiftc`. SwiftPM does not model application bridging headers directly, so a small C target/module map might be needed if the SwiftPM route is used.

3. **Framework module imports**  
   AppKit is likely to work because the complete macOS SDK is copied. Carbon and some older nested Apple framework modules are more likely to expose Clang module-map incompatibilities on Linux.

4. **Linker differences**  
   `ld64.lld` is not Apple’s `ld`. Lex is simple enough to be a good candidate, but Swift autolinking, Objective-C metadata, deployment-version load commands, or the Zig archive format could reveal unsupported behavior.

5. **Signing**  
   Lex requires a stable signature for Accessibility permission. The current pipeline invokes Apple `codesign`: [build.zig](build.zig#L120-L127). xtool has internal iOS-oriented zsign support, but no public, supported macOS signing command. The dependable approach remains transferring the unsigned app to a Mac and running `codesign` there.

6. **No Linux runtime verification**  
   Compilation success would not prove the menu-bar app, event tap, Accessibility permission, hot key, or login item functionality works. Those require testing on macOS.

## Recommendation

For a **reliable build or release pipeline**, do not adopt xtool for Lex. Use a macOS machine or macOS CI runner for the final Swift compile, signing, and testing, while continuing to run Zig tests on Linux.

For a **bounded technical experiment**, xtool is worth trying only as a Darwin SDK/toolchain provider. The target should initially be:

> Produce an unsigned arm64 `Lex.app` on Linux, transfer it to macOS, ad-hoc sign it with Apple `codesign`, and verify it launches.

That experiment is more promising for Lex than for most macOS apps because Lex already avoids Xcode projects and compiled Apple resources. Nevertheless, it is currently an unsupported cross-compilation path rather than a capability xtool claims to provide.

One additional concern: xtool requires the user to supply an Xcode SDK, and Apple’s SDK license may restrict running it on non-Apple hardware. This should be evaluated separately from technical feasibility.

# Plan: Zig remains the sole workflow entry point

One qualification: **xtool has no command that compiles native macOS apps.** Therefore `zig build` cannot delegate compilation to `xtool dev build`; that command would apply xtool’s iOS packaging logic.

The sound integration is:

```diagram
zig build app-unsigned
        │
        ├──▶ Build macOS liblex.a with Zig
        │
        ├──▶ Call `xtool sdk status`
        │     to verify xtool's Darwin SDK
        │
        ├──▶ Call `swift build`
        │     with --swift-sdk arm64-apple-macosx
        │
        └──▶ Install executable into
              macos/Lex.app/Contents/MacOS/Lex
```

Thus Zig owns and invokes the workflow; xtool provisions and validates the Darwin SDK, while SwiftPM performs the actual compilation using that SDK.

## 1. Add a minimal internal SwiftPM manifest

Add a root `Package.swift` used only by `build.zig`:

- Declare macOS 26 as the deployment platform.
- Declare one executable product, `Lex`.
- Point its source at `macos/Lex.swift`.
- Exclude the existing `macos/Lex.app` bundle.
- Do not add `xtool.yml`, because that would opt into xtool’s iOS packer.
- Do not restructure the Swift source.

`build.zig` will pass:

- `src/lex.h` through `-import-objc-header`
- Zig’s generated library directory through linker flags
- `-llex`
- xtool’s architecture-specific macOS Swift SDK

This keeps SwiftPM as an internal implementation detail; users still invoke only `zig build`.

## 2. Refactor the host split in `build.zig`

Replace the current early Linux return in [build.zig](build.zig#L47-L63) with separate unsigned-build implementations.

### On macOS

Preserve the current behavior:

- Build `liblex.a` as `ReleaseSafe`.
- Compile with native `swiftc`: [current Swift command](build.zig#L99-L118).
- `zig build app-unsigned` stops before signing.
- `zig build app` and default `zig build` run Apple `codesign`.
- `zig build run` builds, signs, and opens the app.

### On Linux

Implement only `app-unsigned`:

1. Build `liblex.a` for macOS using the Linux host CPU architecture:
   - `aarch64` Linux → `arm64-apple-macosx`
   - `x86_64` Linux → `x86_64-apple-macosx`
2. Run `xtool sdk status` as a preflight.
3. Run approximately:
   ```sh
   swift build \
     --swift-sdk arm64-apple-macosx \
     --scratch-path .zig-cache/lex-swift \
     -c release \
     ...bridging-header and liblex linker arguments...
   ```
4. Use `swift build --show-bin-path` rather than hard-coding SwiftPM’s output layout.
5. After successful compilation:
   - Copy the executable into `macos/Lex.app/Contents/MacOS/Lex`.
   - Remove any stale `macos/Lex.app/Contents/_CodeSignature`.
6. Leave the existing `Info.plist` untouched.

The target’s macOS 26 minimum version will come from `Package.swift`, matching [the bundle metadata](macos/Lex.app/Contents/Info.plist#L17-L20).

## 3. Keep all signed operations macOS-only

On Linux:

- `zig build app-unsigned` — builds the unsigned app.
- `zig build app` — retains the existing macOS-only notice.
- Default `zig build` — retains the existing macOS-only notice.
- `zig build run` — retains the existing macOS-only notice.
- No invocation of `codesign`, zsign, provisioning, notarization, or `open`.

On macOS, signing remains exactly at the existing boundary: [codesign step](build.zig#L120-L132).

## 4. Fail clearly when the Linux toolchain is incomplete

`app-unsigned` will report actionable failures for:

- `xtool` not installed
- xtool Darwin SDK not installed
- `swift` unavailable or incompatible
- unsupported Linux architecture
- Swift/AppKit module-import failure
- `ld64.lld` link failure

It will not automatically download Xcode or install the SDK during every build. SDK setup remains a one-time prerequisite, for example:

```sh
xtool sdk install /path/to/Xcode.xip
xtool sdk status
swift sdk list
```

## 5. Verification

### Linux

```sh
zig fmt build.zig
zig build test
zig build app-unsigned
```

Then verify:

- `Lex.app/Contents/MacOS/Lex` is a Mach-O executable for the expected architecture.
